title: Shear strength of soil and stability of slopes
summary: Everything here rests on the Mohr–Coulomb criterion τ = c + σ′ tan φ, and on the two limiting cases that cover most problems: pure sand (c = 0) and saturated clay tested undrained (φ = 0). The choice of test — UU, CU or CD — is not a laboratory detail but a modelling decision about whether the field problem is short-term or long-term, and questions test exactly that judgement. For slopes, learn the distinction between a cohesionless slope (stable while β < φ, independent of height) and a cohesive one (height-dependent, analysed by Taylor's stability number or the method of slices).

sections.heading: The Mohr–Coulomb criterion
sections.body:
> **τ = c + σ tan φ**   (total stress)
> **τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′**   (effective stress — the fundamental form)

where **c** is **cohesion** and **φ** the **angle of internal friction**. Physically, cohesion is the strength independent of confining pressure (from electrochemical bonding and cementation between clay particles), while friction is the strength proportional to it (from interlocking and sliding resistance between grains).

**Two limiting cases cover most examination problems:**

| Soil | Parameters | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure sand (cohesionless)** | **c = 0**, τ = σ′ tan φ | Strength is **zero at zero confinement** — sand cannot stand in a vertical cut |
| **Saturated clay, undrained** | **φ_u = 0**, τ = c_u | Strength is **independent of confining pressure** — clay can stand vertically for a while |

That pair explains a great deal: a trench in sand collapses immediately unless supported, while one in stiff clay stands unsupported — until it softens.

**Typical values:**

| Soil | φ′ | c′ |
|---|---|---|
| Loose sand | 28 – 32° | 0 |
| **Dense sand / gravel** | **35 – 45°** | 0 |
| Silt | 27 – 35° | small |
| Normally consolidated clay | 20 – 30° | ≈ 0 |
| Over-consolidated clay | 15 – 25° | 10 – 50 kPa |

Note that **φ′ for clay is not zero** — only the *undrained total-stress* angle φ_u is. Confusing φ_u = 0 with φ′ = 0 is a common and serious error, because it makes long-term clay strength vanish.

**Mohr's circle at failure** is tangent to the failure envelope. Two useful consequences:

> The **failure plane** is inclined at **(45° + φ/2)** to the major principal plane
> **σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2)**

For **φ = 0** the failure plane is at **45°** and **σ₁ − σ₃ = 2c_u** — so the **unconfined compressive strength q_u = 2c_u**, which is why a UCS test on clay gives the undrained cohesion directly.

**Dilatancy** matters for interpreting sand behaviour. **Dense** sand must **expand** to shear (particles ride over one another), so it shows a **peak strength then softens** to a **critical state**. **Loose** sand **contracts** and reaches its strength without a peak. Both converge on the same **critical state friction angle** — which is why the peak φ of a dense sand is a **loading-history property**, not a permanent one, and should be used cautiously in design.

sections.heading: The shear tests and choosing between them
sections.body:
| Test | Controls drainage? | Measures u? | Failure plane |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direct shear (shear box)** | **No** | No | **Predetermined** — may not be the weakest |
| **Triaxial compression** | **Yes** | **Yes** | Free to develop |
| **Unconfined compression** | No (undrained) | No | Free |
| **Vane shear** | No (undrained) | No | Cylindrical |

The **triaxial test is the most versatile** precisely because it controls drainage and can measure pore pressure, so it yields **either total or effective** stress parameters as the problem requires.

**The three triaxial procedures**, and the field situation each models:

| Test | Consolidation | Shearing | Models |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UU (unconsolidated undrained)** | None | **Undrained**, fast | **Immediate (end of construction)** stability — an embankment built quickly on soft clay |
| **CU (consolidated undrained)** | Full, under σ₃ | Undrained, with **u measured** | **Sudden loading or drawdown** after the soil has consolidated |
| **CD (consolidated drained)** | Full | **Drained**, very slow | **Long-term** stability — a permanent cutting or a natural slope |

**This is the substance of the topic.** The choice is not a laboratory preference but a **modelling decision**: is the field loading fast relative to the soil's drainage, or slow?

> **In sand**, drainage is so fast that **all loading is effectively drained** — use effective stress parameters always.
> **In clay**, drainage is so slow that **rapid loading is undrained** — so the critical case may be either short-term or long-term, and both must be checked.

**Which is critical, and when?** For a **loaded** clay (a foundation, an embankment) the **short-term undrained** case is critical, because consolidation subsequently *strengthens* the soil. For an **unloaded** clay (a cutting, an excavation) the **long-term drained** case is critical, because swelling subsequently *weakens* it. That asymmetry explains why cuttings in clay can fail years after construction, and it is a favourite examination point.

**The vane shear test** gives the **undrained strength of soft, sensitive clay in situ**, where an undisturbed sample cannot be recovered at all:

> **c_u = T / [πD²(H/2 + D/6)]**

It also gives **sensitivity** = undisturbed ÷ remoulded strength, by re-shearing the same soil.

**Pore pressure parameters (Skempton):**

> **Δu = B[Δσ₃ + A(Δσ₁ − Δσ₃)]**

with **B = 1 for a fully saturated soil**. A measured B below 1 means the specimen is not fully saturated — a check on test quality before the results are used at all.

sections.heading: Slope stability — cohesionless and cohesive slopes
sections.body:
**An infinite cohesionless slope** is the simplest and most instructive case:

> **F = tan φ / tan β**

So the slope is **stable while β < φ**, and — the striking result — **independent of the height**. A sand slope at its angle of repose is equally stable whether it is 1 m or 100 m high, because both the driving and resisting forces scale with the same weight.

With **seepage parallel to the slope** the factor of safety falls to about **F = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β)** — roughly **halved**, since γ′/γ_sat ≈ 0.5. That is the quantitative reason monsoon seepage triggers so many failures in Nepal's granular hill slopes.

**A cohesive slope is height-dependent**, because cohesion provides a strength that does not scale with the weight:

> **Stability number S_n = c / (F γ H)**

**Taylor's stability charts** give S_n against the slope angle and the depth factor. The **critical height** for a vertical cut in pure clay is

> **H_c = 4c/γ**  (and the theoretical unsupported depth is 2c/γ)

which is why a trench in stiff clay stands unsupported to a few metres and then fails — often without warning, and often after rain has softened it.

**Types of failure** in a cohesive slope, distinguished by where the failure surface emerges:

| Type | Surface |
|---|---|
| **Face (slope) failure** | Emerges **above** the toe |
| **Toe failure** | Passes **through** the toe |
| **Base failure** | Passes **below** the toe, through the foundation soil |

Base failure occurs where a **weak stratum underlies** the slope, and is the most damaging because it involves a much larger mass.

**Methods of analysis:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Swedish circle / ordinary method of slices (Fellenius)** | Ignores inter-slice forces — simple and **conservative** |
| **Bishop's simplified** | Satisfies **vertical** equilibrium of each slice — **more accurate**, the standard |
| **Friction circle** | For c–φ soils, graphical |
| **Taylor's charts** | Rapid, for simple homogeneous slopes |
| Morgenstern–Price, Spencer | Rigorous, satisfy all equilibrium conditions |

The **method of slices** divides the assumed failure mass into vertical slices and takes moments about the centre of the trial circle:

> **F = Σ(c·Δl + N tan φ) / Σ(W sin α)**

The analysis must be repeated for **many trial circles** to find the **critical** one giving the lowest F — a search, not a single calculation, which is why the work is now done by software.

**Total or effective stress?** Use **undrained (total stress, φ = 0)** analysis for the **short-term** case, and **effective stress** analysis with the pore pressure from a flow net or a **pore pressure ratio r_u = u/γh** for the **long-term** case. Mixing the two — using effective parameters with total stresses — is a serious and common error.

**Critical cases for an earth dam**, since they are examined directly:

| Slope | Critical condition |
|---|---|
| **Upstream** | **Sudden drawdown** — the supporting water is removed while pore pressures inside are still high |
| **Downstream** | **Steady seepage** at full reservoir |
| Both | **End of construction**, for a clay core with high construction pore pressures |

Minimum factors of safety are typically **1.5** for the long-term case and **1.2–1.3** for transient cases such as drawdown or seismic loading.

sections.heading: Landslides, liquefaction and stabilisation
sections.body:
**Why slopes fail** — the causes divide neatly into those that **increase the driving force** and those that **reduce the resisting force**:

| Increase driving force | Reduce resisting force |
|---|---|
| Added **surcharge** at the crest (fill, buildings, spoil) | **Rising pore pressure** — rainfall, seepage, a leaking canal |
| **Steepening** by excavation at the toe | **Weathering and softening** over time |
| **Seismic** acceleration | **Loss of cohesion** on saturation |
| Water in tension cracks | **Progressive failure** and strain softening |
| Rapid **drawdown** | Root loss from **deforestation** |

**Toe excavation and crest loading are the two most common human causes** — and both are avoidable. Cutting the toe of a slope to widen a road, or dumping spoil at the crest, are routine practices in Nepali hill construction and routine causes of failure.

**Rainfall is the dominant natural trigger**, and the mechanism is effective stress: infiltration raises u, which lowers σ′, which lowers τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′. Nothing about the soil changes except the water.

**Stabilisation measures**, organised by which side of the equation they address:

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Drainage** — surface drains, catch water drains, sub-horizontal drains, relief wells | **Lowers pore pressure** — the most effective and cheapest measure |
| **Flattening** the slope, **benching** | Reduces the driving force |
| **Toe weighting**, a berm or buttress | Increases the resisting moment |
| **Retaining structures** — gravity wall, gabion, crib, soil nails, anchors | Provides external resistance |
| **Reinforced soil**, geogrids | Adds tensile strength within the mass |
| **Vegetation / bio-engineering** | Roots reinforce, foliage intercepts rain, transpiration dries the soil |
| **Grouting, lime or cement stabilisation** | Increases c and φ |

**Drainage first, always.** It addresses the actual trigger, costs least, and works on the whole mass rather than a local strip. A retaining wall built without drainage often fails, because the hydrostatic pressure behind it was the real problem.

**Bio-engineering** deserves emphasis for Nepal: planting on hill slopes with grasses, shrubs and small structures is a low-cost, locally maintainable technique promoted by the Department of Roads, and it works precisely because it attacks both water and reinforcement together.

**Liquefaction** is a distinct failure mechanism, not a slope failure. It occurs in **loose, saturated, fine to medium sand** under **cyclic (earthquake) loading**: cyclic shearing tries to densify the sand, the water cannot escape quickly, pore pressure rises until **σ′ → 0**, and the soil behaves as a heavy liquid.

| Susceptible | Not susceptible |
|---|---|
| **Loose** sand and silty sand | Dense sand (it dilates rather than contracts) |
| **Saturated**, shallow water table | Dry or partly saturated soil |
| **Uniform fine sand** (low C_u) | Well-graded or gravelly soil (drains fast) |
| Recent, geologically young deposits | Clay (cohesion resists it) |

Consequences: **loss of bearing capacity** (buildings sink or tilt), **flotation** of buried tanks and pipes, **lateral spreading**, and **sand boils** at the surface.

This is a first-order concern in Nepal. **Widespread liquefaction occurred in the Kathmandu Valley in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake**, because the valley is a former lake basin with young, loose, saturated sediments and a shallow water table. **NBC 105:2020** requires liquefaction assessment for susceptible sites.

**Mitigation:** **densification** (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, stone columns), **drainage** to allow pressure dissipation, **lowering the water table**, **grouting**, or **deep foundations** taken through the liquefiable layer to a firm stratum below.

formulas.label: Mohr–Coulomb criterion
formulas.expression: τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′     (sand: c = 0;  saturated clay undrained: φ_u = 0, τ = c_u)
formulas.note: φ_u = 0 is the undrained TOTAL stress angle. φ′ for clay is NOT zero.

formulas.label: Principal stress relation at failure
formulas.expression: σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2);   failure plane at (45° + φ/2)
formulas.note: For φ = 0: σ₁ − σ₃ = 2c_u, so unconfined strength q_u = 2c_u and the failure plane is at 45°.

formulas.label: Infinite cohesionless slope
formulas.expression: F = tan φ / tan β     (with seepage parallel to slope, F ≈ (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β))
formulas.note: Independent of HEIGHT. Seepage roughly halves the factor of safety.

formulas.label: Taylor's stability number
formulas.note: A cohesive slope IS height-dependent, unlike a cohesionless one.

formulas.label: Critical height of a vertical cut in clay
formulas.note: Why a trench in stiff clay stands for a while and then fails, often after rain.

formulas.label: Method of slices
formulas.expression: F = Σ(c·Δl + N tan φ) / Σ(W sin α)
formulas.note: Repeat for many trial circles to find the critical one. Bishop's method adds vertical equilibrium.

formulas.label: Vane shear strength
formulas.note: For soft sensitive clay in situ. Re-shearing gives sensitivity = undisturbed / remoulded.

formulas.label: Skempton's pore pressure parameters
formulas.note: B = 1 for full saturation; a lower measured B means the specimen was not saturated.
